contentBlocks.text: You've learned inertia and F=ma. Today: what happens when two objects push on each other!

Newton's Third Law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force — when object A pushes on object B, object B simultaneously pushes back on object A with equal strength in the opposite direction. When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force, which is why your hand doesn't simply pass through it. Identify the action-reaction pair when a swimmer pushes backward against the water to swim forward.
You just learned Newton's Third Law! Tomorrow we'll combine all three laws in a real-world application.

objectives: State Newton's Third Law: equal and opposite action-reaction force pairs
Identify the action-reaction pair in a swimmer pushing against water
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's First and Second Law work.
2. Introduce the Third Law using the wall-push example.
3. Have the child identify the swimmer's action-reaction pair.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's combined-laws application.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use the wall-push example again with the swimmer, explicitly naming which push is the 'action' and which is the 'reaction'
Ready for more: ask the child why a rocket can accelerate in the vacuum of space, where there's no air to push against, using the Third Law
A commonly confused law — worth emphasizing that BOTH forces in the pair act on DIFFERENT objects, not the same one
teacherGuide.answerKey: The action force is the swimmer pushing backward against the water; the reaction force is the water pushing forward against the swimmer with equal strength, which is what actually propels the swimmer forward through the water.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 9-12 Physical Science standard HS-PS2-1, continuing this week's thread with Newton's Third Law.
